title: The Lowering Phase Is Part of the Rep—not a Countdown
subtitle: A controlled return matters. But the evidence does not say every repetition needs to move in slow motion.
imageAlt: Two friends in a bright home gym compare notes after each performs a comfortable dumbbell row, one lowering the weight smoothly while the other observes without coaching.
imageConcept: A relaxed, eye-level scene of two friends sharing a home workout: one completes a light dumbbell row with a steady, unhurried lowering phase while the other watches and holds a small training notebook. Their expressions are curious, not competitive; the weight is manageable and the room feels accessible.
body:
In a strength exercise, attention often goes to the effortful part: standing up from a squat, pressing a weight overhead, or pulling a handle toward the body. The return can feel like the space between repetitions. Yet that lowering phase is still part of the movement. In a squat, it is the descent; in a dumbbell row, it is letting the weight travel back toward the floor; in a push-up, it is the way down. If the weight drops, swings or rebounds, you have less control over that portion of the rep.

That does not mean the answer is to make every descent painstakingly slow. A steady, manageable return is a useful way to practise the whole movement. Counting four or five seconds on every repetition is a different choice—one that may suit a particular exercise or person, but is not automatically a better route to strength or muscle growth. The helpful question is not, “Did I make this rep last long enough?” It is, “Could I guide the weight back through the range I intended?”
Controlled is not the same as slow

“Controlled” describes what you can manage; “slow” describes pace. They can overlap, but they are not synonyms. A repetition can be deliberately slow and still lose position, while a smooth, uncounted return can remain composed. The goal is not to make the lowering phase look theatrical. It is to avoid surrendering the movement to momentum when the exercise calls for control.

Research on repetition tempo has tested a range of speeds, rather than identifying one ideal count for every lift. A 2025 systematic review and meta-analysis included 14 studies in healthy adults that compared training tempos while controlling other training variables. Across the tempos studied, the researchers found minimal overall difference in muscle growth; the estimates varied, so the finding does not establish that every pace is interchangeable in every programme [1]. That is a measured result, not a reason to ignore technique or abandon a pace that helps you train well. It does challenge the simple claim that slower is always better.

The American College of Sports Medicine’s 2026 position stand synthesized 137 systematic reviews, covering more than 30,000 participants. Among its findings, time under tension did not consistently affect training outcomes [2]. That broad conclusion does not prescribe a particular lowering speed. Nor does it mean that how a repetition feels or looks is irrelevant: the review addresses training outcomes across many prescriptions, not every practical question a person may have about controlling a specific movement.

It is also important to separate tempo from eccentric-focused training. The eccentric action is the muscle-lengthening part of a movement under load; in a conventional curl, that is lowering the dumbbell. But a programme that emphasizes eccentric work may involve different exercise choices, loading, assistance or training structure—not merely counting slowly on the way down. A review comparing eccentric-focused with concentric-focused training found no statistically significant overall difference in hypertrophy, while rating the evidence very low and noting substantial variation across studies [3]. Those findings cannot be reduced to “slow negatives build more muscle,” or used to promise that one ordinary tempo is best.
Try a smoother return on a familiar exercise

If you want to explore this without turning a workout into a tempo test, choose an exercise you already know and a weight you can manage comfortably. A body-weight squat, light dumbbell row, or seated cable row can work. Don’t use a new or unusually heavy lift for your first experiment. If you have been given specific guidance for an injury or health condition, follow that rather than this general practice.

Start with a small set at your usual pace. Notice whether the return is smooth and whether you can stop it where you intend, without dropping, bouncing or twisting to get there. On the next set, keep the same load and try guiding the weight back with a little more attention. Let the motion take the time it naturally needs; there is no required count. Keep the rest of your setup steady, and finish the set if you cannot maintain the movement you chose. The point is to compare sensations and control—not to force a slower performance or prove anything to a training partner.

A count is a tool, not a standard you must meet. It may be useful when you are learning a movement, want a reminder not to rush, or are following a programme that deliberately uses tempo. If you choose one, make it a simple cue: for example, think “smoothly back” or count lightly rather than trying to stretch each repetition to the longest possible duration. If the count makes you tense, distracts you from posture, or turns the set into a race against an internal clock, drop it.

Different exercises also offer different opportunities to control the return. With a light dumbbell, you may be able to guide the full path easily. With a challenging lift, the movement may naturally be faster or harder to regulate. That is not an automatic sign of failure. Use a load and range of motion that let you perform the exercise as intended, and adjust the exercise or ask a qualified professional if you are unsure how to do that safely. There is no need to bolt a slow-lowering rule onto every movement in your programme.
Notice the movement, not just the number

A practical way to review a set is to name one thing you observed, without scoring yourself. Did the weight return along a steady path? Did your body stay in a position that felt appropriate for the exercise? Was one part harder to manage than another? Those notes can help you decide whether to keep the same load, use a more comfortable range, or ask for guidance. They are more informative than simply recording that every rep lasted a chosen number of seconds.

If you train with someone else, agree on the purpose of their attention before the set. They might watch whether the weight is being lowered smoothly, but they do not need to dictate a pace that feels unnatural to you. Partners can have different proportions, experience, confidence and movement preferences. A useful observation is specific and easy to act on—“the last few returns got faster”—rather than a verdict about someone’s discipline. The lifter remains the person who decides whether to adjust, rest or stop.

The lowering phase deserves attention because it is part of the repetition, not because it holds a secret advantage that can be unlocked by counting slowly. Research to date does not establish that deliberately longer tempos produce superior muscle growth across the board, and studies of eccentric-focused programmes ask a broader question than whether to slow a regular rep. Keep those distinctions clear, and the practical takeaway is straightforward: choose a manageable load, guide the return rather than abandoning it, and use a count only when it helps.

On your next familiar set, try a few repetitions without changing anything else. Let the weight travel back smoothly, at a pace you can control. Then decide whether that attention made the movement clearer or whether your usual rhythm already works. Both answers are useful. Training is not improved by making every repetition elaborate; it is improved by choosing a method you can repeat, adapt and understand.
